strengths: Simple, practical method requiring minimal code changes and computational overhead; easy for practitioners to adopt

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, value-based/actor-critic methods, with proper experimental methodology (multiple seeds, IQM metric, confidence intervals)
Consistent improvements across diverse settings (DQN +18-24%, CQL +20-125%, though more modest for IQN +7%)
Clear ablation study (Figure 1) convincingly demonstrates minimum operator superiority over alternatives (Max, Mean, Random)
Well-written with clear motivation; theoretical convergence proof in tabular setting provides formal justification
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, JAX code snippet, promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: taking the minimum between two estimates is a straightforward application of existing ideas (Maxmin Q-learning); the conceptual contribution is minimal
Theoretical analysis only covers tabular case, far from deep RL setting where MINTO is applied; no insight into why it works with function approximation or when it might fail
Concerning negative/zero results on DMC-Hard (continuous control) inadequately explained; raises questions about universal applicability despite claims of broad effectiveness
Modest improvements in key settings (IQN: ~7%, continuous control: often marginal); while consistent, magnitude is underwhelming in several domains

Incomplete analysis of when/why method works: no investigation of target update frequency T interaction, no systematic characterization of algorithm/domain properties determining effectiveness, no exploration of acknowledged low-noise bias-variance trade-off

Missing practical guidance: unclear which algorithms/domains benefit most; paper doesn't clearly differentiate MINTO from related hybrid methods (ScDQN, FR-DQN) regarding mechanisms and relative merits
Questionable baseline comparisons: Maxmin DQN uses ensembles (N=2) while MINTO uses single networks—comparison may conflate efficiency with fundamental superiority
Individual game results (Figures 7-12, 19) show high variance and modest gains on many tasks; per-task breakdown reveals inconsistent benefits

strengths: Simplicity and Practicality: Minimal code changes required with negligible computational overhead
Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: Extensive benchmarks across online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, and diverse architectures with rigorous statistical reporting
Thorough Ablation Study: Clear comparison of alternative operators (max, mean, random) demonstrating superiority of minimum operator
Consistent Improvements: Performance gains across diverse settings suggests broad applicability
Reproducibility: Clear pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, and commitment to code release
weaknesses: Limited Novelty: Using minimums for overestimation correction is well-established (Double Q-learning, CDQ). The contribution—applying min to target computation rather than action selection—is incremental with insufficient conceptual differentiation from prior work
Weak Theoretical Analysis: Convergence proof limited to tabular setting; lacks analysis of why min works in deep RL function approximation, convergence rates, or bias-variance tradeoffs
Modest Empirical Improvements: IQN improvements (~7-10%), many continuous control gains within confidence intervals, suggesting limited practical significance despite consistency
Poor Actor-Critic Performance: Acknowledges negligible or negative gains on DMC-Hard, undermining claims of broad applicability to modern deep RL where actor-critic methods are standard

Unexplained Inconsistencies: CQL shows 125% improvement with CNN but only 20% with IMPALA (same algorithm, different architecture)—raises questions about method reliability and architecture dependence
Insufficient Analysis of Method Behavior: Limited discussion of why online selection ratio varies (0-45%), when method fails, or why single-critic variant required for best results

Motivation Issues: Conceptual confusion about using min to reduce overestimation when online networks increase overestimation; actual mechanism (conservative targets) is obvious but not deeply motivated
Missing Theoretical Insight: No explanation for why min is appropriate beyond empirical ablation; lacks principled understanding of when/why method works

strengths: Simple and practical implementation requiring minimal code changes
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse settings (15 Atari games, IQN, CQL, 26 continuous control tasks)
Consistent improvements demonstrated across online/offline RL and discrete/continuous control
Thorough reproducibility measures with code availability, hyperparameter documentation, and multiple random seeds
Well-executed experimental methodology using appropriate metrics (IQM, confidence intervals, multiple architectures)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution (min between two Q-estimates) exists in CDQ and Maxmin Q-learning; applying specifically to online/target networks is incremental

Weak theoretical analysis: convergence proof only applies to tabular setting while all experiments use deep RL with function approximation; proof is routine application of existing framework without new insights
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: claims that min reduces overestimation bias lack rigorous justification; circular reasoning that min selects lower values therefore reduces bias
Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: 7-10% for IQN, mixed results on DMC-Hard, often within confidence interval overlap; no characterization of when method helps vs fails

Missing analysis of fundamental design choice: no principled explanation for why min is optimal beyond empirical ablation; strong role for target network (55% selection rate) contradicts 'use online network' framing
Insufficient differentiation from related work: relationship to CDQ and ScQL underexplored; claim of orthogonality needs deeper analysis
Actor-critic integration requires multiple design variants suggesting limited general applicability; single-critic works best but lacks explanation
No practical guidance: when should practitioners choose MINTO over alternatives like CDQ or Double DQN?
Gaps in experimental analysis: online selection ratios only shown for one game; no ablation on target update frequency interaction; baseline tuning fairness unclear

strengths: Exceptional empirical validation across 100+ environments spanning online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, and multiple algorithms with rigorous statistical reporting (IQM, confidence intervals, 5-10 seeds per task)
Simplicity and practicality: single-line code modification with negligible overhead, no new hyperparameters, seamlessly integrates into existing methods across value-based and actor-critic approaches
Excellent reproducibility: released code with JAX implementation, complete hyperparameter specifications, per-task breakdowns, and standard public benchmarks enabling verification and adoption

Comprehensive analysis including strong ablations (Figure 1) demonstrating superiority of min operator, convergence proof via Generalized Q-learning framework, online selection ratio tracking, and value estimation/bias analysis

Consistent and substantial improvements on discrete control (Atari): ~17% improvement with CNN and ~22% with IMPALA+LayerNorm over DQN, with improvements generalizing across IQN, CQL, and other algorithms
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applying established min(Q₁, Q₂) principle to online/target networks rather than independent networks is incremental; relationship to Maxmin DQN and Double Q-learning not sufficiently differentiated

Weak theoretical justification: convergence proof restricted to tabular setting using straightforward application of existing Generalized Q-learning framework; no formal analysis of why min(Q_online, Q_target) mitigates overestimation in function approximation regime where most benefits occur

Inconsistent results undermine broad applicability claims: DMC-Hard continuous control shows no improvement (Figure 7), IQN improvements (~10%) substantially smaller than DQN (~17-22%), and continuous control gains are modest and task-dependent

Fundamental contradiction in proposed mechanism: paper argues MINTO reduces overestimation bias, yet Figure 35 shows MINTO actually underestimates on Car-on-Hill; connection between actual underestimation and improved performance not adequately explained

Critical design choices lack justification: no analysis of why specifically min (only empirical ablation), no discussion of stop_gradient necessity on online estimates (line 8, Listing 1), no sensitivity analysis to target update frequency T, missing ablations on update strategies

Incomplete analysis of failure modes: no explanation for DMC-Hard underperformance, no guidance on when practitioners should use MINTO versus standard methods, no analysis of task properties predicting effectiveness
